extracted.intended_audience: implementation researchers, health service managers, clinicians, and health technology developers
extracted.subtask_description: Using the NASSS framework to predict, evaluate, and plan for adoption, nonadoption, scale-up, spread, and sustainability of technology-supported health and social care programs. Focuses on domains such as the condition, adopters, organization, wider context, and long-term adaptation.

rubrics_metrics.name: 4A. Adoption by staff
rubrics_metrics.description: Adoption (and continued use) of the technology by staff; nonadoption or abandonment may occur.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Nonadoption was sometimes explained by technology attributes (eg, usability or ease of use) but more commonly by staff concerns about threats to their scope of practice, concerns for patient safety and welfare, or fear of job loss. Evaluate staff engagement, perceived threats, and reasons for resistance.

rubrics_metrics.name: 4B. Adoption by patients/clients
rubrics_metrics.description: Adoption, acceptance (including symbolic meaning and aesthetics), and the work required of patients or clients to use the technology.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess the burden placed on patients, aesthetic and symbolic acceptability, and whether intended users are willing and able to do the required work to use the technology.

rubrics_metrics.name: 4C. Assumptions about lay caregivers
rubrics_metrics.description: Assumptions built into the technology or service model about the availability and behavior of lay caregivers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many cases of nonuse were explained by weak or absent social networks, limited IT skills and distrust among lay caregivers, or long-standing family conflicts; technologies sometimes surfaced but did not solve these issues. Check whether the design presumes support that does not exist.

rubrics_metrics.name: 5A. Organisation's capacity to embrace service-level innovation
rubrics_metrics.description: The organisation’s capacity to embrace any service-level innovation (antecedent conditions and structural capacity).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case studies showed a wide range of antecedent conditions and levels of capacity which influenced uptake and internal scale-up. Consider organisational structures, staffing, and slack resources needed for innovation.

rubrics_metrics.name: 5B. Organisation's readiness for a specific technology
rubrics_metrics.description: The organisation’s readiness for a particular technology (practical preparedness for implementation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Readiness varies and influences uptake. Evaluate whether the organisation is prepared for required changes in workflows, roles, skills, and infrastructure for that specific technology.

rubrics_metrics.name: 5C. Adoption decision and business modeling
rubrics_metrics.description: The adoption decision (often a board-level decision to allocate a budget line) and the viability of business modelling for the technology-supported program.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Three main problems identified: (1) lack of data — uptake/use/impact predictions often overoptimistic; (2) lack of money — organisations may not recognize need for dedicated implementation/maintenance budget beyond technology cost; (3) interdependencies between organisations/teams. Assess business case realism and funding for ongoing implementation and maintenance.

rubrics_metrics.name: 5D. Disruption to established work routines
rubrics_metrics.description: The extent to which established work routines will be disrupted or made too brittle by the new technology.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There may be a transition period with parallel routines (including legacy systems) before replacement. Evaluate brittleness, risk of disruption, need for bridging/workarounds, and potential for parallel processes during transition.

rubrics_metrics.name: 5E. Work involved in implementation and who will do it
rubrics_metrics.description: The amount and distribution of work required to implement the technology and who is responsible for that work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implementation work is extensive, often hidden and typically underestimated. Levels described range from: established shared vision with few simple tasks; some work needed to build shared vision and enact new practices; to significant work needed to build shared vision, engage staff, enact new practices, and monitor impact. Implementation requires 'taming' the technology through tinkering/domesticating, sense making/coherence work, and building a realistic shared vision of capabilities and limits.

rubrics_metrics.name: 6A. The wider context (political, economic, regulatory, professional, sociocultural)
rubrics_metrics.description: The political, economic, regulatory, professional (eg, medico-legal), and sociocultural context for program rollout.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wider context can be pivotal for moving from successful demonstration to mainstreamed service. Consider national financial and regulatory requirements, funding approval mechanisms (eg, tariffs/reimbursement), positions of professional bodies and defense societies, legal/regulatory challenges, and stakeholder support or opposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: 7A. Scope for adapting and coevolving technology and service over time
rubrics_metrics.description: The degree of scope for adapting and coevolving the technology and the service as local need or context changes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scenarios range from strong scope for adaptation and embedding to limited/uncertain potential to significant barriers to adaptation/co-evolution. Note that adaptation of staff roles and care pathways can be difficult where subcontractor relationships constrain change.

rubrics_metrics.name: 7B. Organisational resilience and reflexive monitoring
rubrics_metrics.description: How resilient the organisation is to handling critical events and adapting to unforeseen eventualities; capacity for reflexive monitoring.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Important functions include sense making, collective reflection, and adaptive action (macrocognitive functions). Organisations may encourage or discourage these. Evaluate ability to detect critical events/issues and respond through coordinated action; assess whether reflexive monitoring is practiced.

rubrics_metrics.name: Complexity classification of NASSS domains (simple/complicated/complex)
rubrics_metrics.description: Heuristic classification of each domain as simple, complicated, or complex.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The framework advises classifying domains on this axis and notes that complexity in multiple domains poses the greatest challenge to scale-up, spread, and sustainability. It cautions that the framework cannot be applied deterministically — interactions differ by case and setting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fit to condition / modelling of the illness or problem
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the technology and linked program are designed around an accurate, context-sensitive model of the condition/problem they aim to address.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A striking failure mode was design around an oversimplified, textbook model of the condition. Assess whether the underlying clinical/condition model matches real-world variability and complexity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prototyping, customisability, dependability, and data suitability
rubrics_metrics.description: Quality attributes of the technology: sufficiency of prototyping, ability to customise, dependability, and whether it generates appropriate, complete, and contestation-resistant data/knowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failures were linked to technologies that were insufficiently prototyped, insufficiently customizable, insufficiently dependable, required complex knowledge to use, or generated incomplete/inappropriate/contested data. Evaluate robustness, usability, customization, and data validity for the care context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity of the value proposition
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the technology has a clear value proposition for the developer (viable business venture) and for patients (clear benefit) along with an affordable real-world service model.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unclear value propositions undermined uptake and sustainability. Assess both commercial and patient-facing value, and whether a viable, affordable service delivery model exists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Users' (personal/professional) reasons to resist
rubrics_metrics.description: Plausible personal or professional reasons intended users might have to resist or reject the technology.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Intended users may resist for legitimate reasons (eg, professional identity, workload, perceived risk). Identify and address these reasons rather than assuming resistance is irrational.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organisational setup for innovation and ability to support implementation work
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether organisations are adequately set up for innovation and able to support the extensive, often hidden work required to implement and sustain change.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Problems include organisations not ready/interested in innovation, inability to negotiate viable business models with partners, inability to shift to new ways of working, and inability to support the extensive implementation work (including rhetorical 'sense-making' work). Assess capacity to provide leadership, resources, governance, and ongoing operational support.

rubrics_metrics.name: External complexity (financial, regulatory, legal, policy), especially reimbursement
rubrics_metrics.description: Complexity in external systems — financial, regulatory, legal, and policy environments — that affect mainstreaming and spread, with reimbursement being particularly key.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such external complexities can stall mainstreaming and spread. Examine reimbursement mechanisms, legal/regulatory constraints, fiscal policy, and other macro-level factors that affect feasibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Long-term adaptability to remain clinically, operationally, and financially viable
rubrics_metrics.description: Ability of the program to adapt and evolve over time in ways that continue to meet users’ needs and remain clinically, operationally, and financially viable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Programs that cannot adapt risk failing to sustain adoption or scale. Use formative and summative evaluations with multiple methods, narrative accounts, and imagination to capture interdependencies, nonlinear effects, and unintended consequences.
